name: George Washington
info: George Washington was a Virginia planter who commanded the Continental Army in the American Revolutionary War, presided over the Constitutional Convention of 1787 and served as the first president of the United States from 1789 to 1797.

facts.born: 22 February 1732 (Old Style 11 February 1731), at Popes Creek in Westmoreland County, Virginia; the first of six children of Augustine and Mary Ball Washington
facts.died: 14 December 1799, at Mount Vernon, Virginia, of a throat illness; modern medical authors have largely concluded that it was probably severe epiglottitis, complicated by bloodletting and other treatments
facts.role: Commander of the Virginia Regiment (1755–1758); member of the Virginia House of Burgesses (from 1758); commander-in-chief of the Continental Army (1775–1783); president of the Constitutional Convention (1787); first president of the United States (1789–1797)
facts.known: Leading the Continental Army to victory in the Revolutionary War; crossing the Delaware and the battles of Trenton and Princeton; the siege of Yorktown; resigning his command in 1783; presiding over the Constitutional Convention; setting the precedents of the presidency; the Farewell Address of 1796; owning slaves and providing in his will for their freedom

t: A Virginia surveyor, militia officer and planter, Washington was made commander-in-chief of the Continental Army in 1775 and held a poorly equipped force together until the British surrender at Yorktown in 1781.

He gave up his command in 1783, presided over the Constitutional Convention in 1787 and, as the first president from 1789 to 1797, set lasting precedents for the office, among them retirement after two terms.
He owned slaves all his adult life and freed those he owned outright only by his will, and his campaigns and policies towards Native Americans have drawn sharply different judgements from historians.
dyk: Washington left mainland North America only once, in 1751, when he went with his half-brother Lawrence to Barbados. He caught smallpox there, which left his face slightly scarred and made him immune to the disease.
ev: George Washington is born on 22 February at Popes Creek in Westmoreland County, Virginia
As a lieutenant colonel of the Virginia Regiment he ambushes a French detachment on 28 May and surrenders Fort Necessity in July, the affair that ignited the French and Indian War
He marries the wealthy widow Martha Dandridge Custis on 6 January and settles at Mount Vernon
The Continental Congress unanimously elects him commander-in-chief of the Continental Army in June
He crosses the Delaware River and surprises the Hessian garrison at Trenton at sunrise on 26 December
With the French under Rochambeau he besieges Yorktown, where the British surrender on 19 October
He is unanimously elected to preside over the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia
Unanimously elected the first president, he takes the oath of office at Federal Hall in New York City on 30 April

sections.early:
George Washington was born on 22 February 1732 at Popes Creek in Westmoreland County, Virginia, the first of six children of Augustine and Mary Ball Washington. His father, a justice of the peace, had four more children from a first marriage; among them George was closest to his older half-brother Lawrence. The family settled at Ferry Farm near Fredericksburg in 1738. When Augustine died in 1743, George inherited Ferry Farm and ten slaves, and Lawrence inherited the plantation he renamed Mount Vernon. The death cost George the schooling in England that his half-brothers had received. He learned mathematics and land surveying and became a talented draftsman and mapmaker.

William Fairfax, Lawrence's father-in-law, became his patron and surrogate father. In 1748 Washington spent a month with a team surveying Fairfax's land in the Shenandoah Valley; the next year he received a surveyor's licence from the College of William & Mary and was appointed surveyor of Culpeper County, a post he resigned in 1750. By 1752 he owned 2,315 acres. In 1751 he left mainland North America for the only time, going with Lawrence to Barbados in the hope that the climate would cure his brother's tuberculosis; there he contracted smallpox. Lawrence died in 1752, and Washington leased Mount Vernon from his widow, inheriting it outright in 1761. Lawrence's service as adjutant general of the Virginia militia inspired him to seek a commission, and the lieutenant governor, Robert Dinwiddie, made him a major.
sections.rise:
In October 1753 Dinwiddie sent Washington to demand that the French vacate land claimed by the British; the French refused, and his published report brought him a measure of distinction. Promoted lieutenant colonel of the Virginia Regiment in February 1754, he ambushed a French detachment of about 50 men on 28 May. Its commander, Joseph Coulon de Jumonville, who had been carrying a diplomatic message, was killed. On 3 July the French attacked Fort Necessity and Washington surrendered, signing a document in French in which he unwittingly took responsibility for "assassinating" Jumonville. The affair ignited the French and Indian War. In 1755 he served as an aide to General Edward Braddock and rallied the survivors of the Battle of the Monongahela. He commanded the Virginia Regiment from August 1755, was refused a royal commission, and resigned in 1758.

On 6 January 1759 he married Martha Dandridge Custis, a wealthy widow, which made him one of the wealthiest men in Virginia. He sat in the House of Burgesses from 1758 and became a prominent critic of British taxation, proposing a boycott of British goods in May 1769. He called the Coercive Acts "an invasion of our rights and privileges" and in 1774 was chosen a delegate to the First Continental Congress. After the war broke out on 19 April 1775, Congress created the Continental Army on 14 June; John Adams nominated Washington as its commander-in-chief, mainly for his military experience and in the belief that a Virginian would better unite the colonies. He was unanimously elected the next day and declined a salary.
sections.deeds:
Washington forced the British to evacuate Boston on 17 March 1776 but was beaten at the Battle of Long Island and driven from New York; his army, reduced to 5,400 men, retreated through New Jersey. He crossed the Delaware and surprised the Hessians at Trenton on 26 December 1776, then struck at Princeton on 3 January 1777, victories that revived Patriot morale. He lost at Brandywine and Germantown later that year and wintered at Valley Forge, where between 2,000 and 3,000 men died of disease and want. He had his soldiers inoculated against smallpox. On 19 October 1781 a French and American force under his command took the surrender of over 7,000 British soldiers at Yorktown. After the Treaty of Paris of 3 September 1783 he disbanded the army and resigned his commission that December.

He was unanimously elected to preside over the Constitutional Convention, which opened in Philadelphia on 25 May 1787; the Constitution was signed on 17 September. Unanimously chosen as president by the electors, he was inaugurated in New York City on 30 April 1789 and re-elected in 1793. He preferred the title "Mr. President" to the majestic styles proposed by the Senate, formed a cabinet that included Thomas Jefferson and Alexander Hamilton, selected the first justices of the Supreme Court and backed Hamilton's financial programme. On 22 April 1793 he proclaimed American neutrality in the French Revolutionary Wars. He commanded in person the militia that suppressed the Whiskey Rebellion and supported the Jay Treaty with Britain, signed on 19 November 1794.
sections.opponents:
Washington's command was questioned during the war. After his defeats in 1777 and the victory of General Horatio Gates at Saratoga, admiration for him waned; a revolt among his officers prompted some members of Congress to consider removing him, until the matter was dropped. As president he tried to stay above party, but his advisers split into Hamilton's Federalists and Jefferson's Republicans, and his support for Hamilton's agenda brought bitter controversy. Jefferson held that the Jay Treaty angered France and "invited rather than avoided" war. In his last months in office a partisan press accused him of being ambitious and greedy, and Republicans including James Madison called the Farewell Address an anti-French campaign document.

During his lifetime at least 577 slaves lived and worked at Mount Vernon. He grew to oppose slavery from the 1760s, but as president he stayed publicly silent and, critics note, did not initiate or support any measure to end it, remaining dependent on slave labour; this has led to calls to remove his name and statues from public places. During the war he ordered an expedition against the Haudenosaunee, allies of the British, that destroyed their villages. The historian Colin G. Calloway wrote that he "had a lifelong obsession with getting Indian land" and began policies and campaigns with "devastating effects in Indian country", whereas his biographer Ron Chernow describes him as trying to be even-handed and as never advocating outright confiscation of tribal land.
sections.last:
Washington did not feel bound to a limit of two terms, but he was dismayed by the personal attacks on him and wanted a truly contested election to be held. His Farewell Address, drafted with James Madison and extensively rewritten by Hamilton, was published on 19 September 1796. It put national identity first, warned against political parties and against entangling foreign alliances, and advised against involvement in European wars. He retired to Mount Vernon in March 1797. Nearly all his wealth lay in land and slaves, not ready cash, and he built a whiskey distillery worked by enslaved people to add to his income. In retirement he became a more committed Federalist and vocally supported the Alien and Sedition Acts. During the "Quasi-War" with France, President John Adams nominated him commander of the armies on 4 July 1798; he served until his death, leaving active leadership to Hamilton.

On 12 December 1799 he inspected his farms on horseback for five hours in bad weather. Two days later he woke with an inflamed throat and difficulty breathing. He was bled, in all approximately five pints, and his condition worsened; he died between 10 and 11 p.m. on 14 December 1799, his wife at the foot of the bed. His last words were "'Tis well." Accusations of medical malpractice have persisted, and modern medical authors have largely concluded that he probably died of severe epiglottitis complicated by his treatment. His will freed his valet Billy Lee, and the rest of the slaves he owned outright upon Martha's death; Martha signed an order to free them on 1 January 1801.
sections.legacy:
Washington is commonly known as the Father of His Country. Henry Lee III eulogised him as "first in war, first in peace, and first in the hearts of his countrymen", and polls have consistently placed him among the highest-ranked presidents. The precedents he set endured: republicanism, a peaceful transfer of power, the title "Mr. President", the cabinet and the two-term tradition. His resignation of his command in 1783 was, in the words of the historian Edward J. Larson, "extolled by later historians as a signal event that set the country's political course". As leader of the first successful revolution against a colonial empire he became an international symbol of liberation and nationalism.

He has been extensively memorialised. The national capital was named for him in 1791, as were a state, the 555-foot Washington Monument dedicated in 1885, and many schools and universities; he appears on Mount Rushmore, on the one-dollar bill and on the quarter. Congress made his birthday a federal holiday in 1879, and in 1976 he was posthumously appointed General of the Armies of the United States. The biography that Mason Locke Weems wrote in 1809 fostered what Chernow calls "enduring myths", such as the story of the cherry tree. In the 21st century his reputation has been critically scrutinised. The historian David Hackett Fischer defined his character as "integrity, self-discipline, courage, absolute honesty, resolve, and decision"; others stress his slaveholding and, in Calloway's account, the dispossession of Indian peoples that the nation's growth demanded.

summary: George Washington led the Continental Army through the American Revolutionary War, presided over the convention that drafted the Constitution and served two terms as the first president of the United States. He set the precedents of the office and gave up power willingly. A slaveholder all his adult life, he freed those he owned only by his will.
references: Ron Chernow, Washington: A Life (Penguin Press, 2010)
Joseph J. Ellis, His Excellency: George Washington (Alfred A. Knopf, 2004)
John E. Ferling, The First of Men: A Life of George Washington (Oxford University Press, 2010)
Colin G. Calloway, The Indian World of George Washington: The First President, the First Americans, and the Birth of the Nation (Oxford University Press, 2018)
Henry Wiencek, An Imperfect God: George Washington, His Slaves, and the Creation of America (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2003)
notes: The article writes dates month-first (American style). In the events' date column I give years only; in the event sentences I kept the article's month-first form ('on December 26'); in the facts and sections I wrote them day-first, as the site's other texts do. Editor to make uniform if wanted.
Birth: the article gives February 22, 1732 with Old Style February 11, 1731; start is 1732.
The Yorktown surrender: the article says the siege ended with a British surrender on October 19, 1781 and also that the signing ceremony took place on October 19 after two days of negotiation.
Re-election: the lead says elected in 1789 and 1792; the body says the Electoral College re-elected him on February 13, 1793. I wrote 're-elected in 1793'.

'forced the British to evacuate Boston on 17 March 1776': the article says he secured the Dorchester Heights 'to try to force the British out' and that on March 17 the evacuation began; the year 1776 comes from the lead ('siege of Boston in March 1776').
'Virginia House of Burgesses (from 1758)': the article says 'for seven years beginning in 1758' and then that he was more active from the 1760s and a delegate in 1774; I did not give an end year.

'Commander of the Virginia Regiment (1755-1758)': he was also its second-in-command and then colonel in 1754 before resigning; the lead says 'from 1754 to 1763', which does not match the body (he resigned in 1758). I followed the body.

Emancipation: the article says both that he 'emancipated 123 or 124 slaves' and that his will freed Billy Lee and 'the rest of his personally owned slaves outright upon Martha's death', with Martha signing an order on January 1, 1801 ('one year after' his death). I gave no number in the text.

'critics note' in the opponents section stands for the article's 'Washington has been criticized for holding enslaved people ... he did not initiate or support any initiatives for bringing about its end.'
The Haudenosaunee expedition: the article gives no date or casualty figures, only that he ordered it and that it destroyed their villages (after the 1778 paragraph).

'died of disease and want' at Valley Forge: the article says the army 'lost between 2,000 and 3,000 men as a result of disease and lack of food, clothing, and shelter' - 'lost' may include more than deaths; editor may prefer 'lost'.
The word 'greatest' in the lead's 'one of the greatest presidents' was avoided; I used the Legacy section's 'among the highest-ranked'.

Death place: the article does not say 'at Mount Vernon' in the death paragraph in so many words, but he fell ill inspecting his farms there, his overseer bled him, and the funeral and burial were at Mount Vernon.

Left out for length (all in the article): the Culper Ring, the bounty-land purchases of 1770 that left some veterans feeling duped, the burial and later reburial, that the couple had no children together.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js, or its Further reading list), chosen by the editor.
